items.excerpt: Anadolu’s recap of top stories from around the globe Diyar Guldogan 29 October 2026• Update: 29 October 2026 WASHINGTON Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Thursday, including Israel’s final vote count, renewed efforts to revive US-Iran talks, Spain mourning one of its deadliest train crashes, North Korea’s missile launches, and Flavio Bolsonaro declaring himself Brazil’s “leader” from the US. More than 500,000 outstanding ballots could reshape Israel’s parliamentary seat distribution as counting continues Thursday, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor its main opposition projected to secure a governing majority. Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats, compared with 48 for the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot and a record combined 19 for predominantly Arab parties, according to Channel 12. A majority requires 61 seats in the 120-member Knesset. The outstanding ballots, cast by soldiers and others voting away from their registered polling stations, were expected to be counted by Thursday evening, Israel’s public broadcaster reported. - Trump confirms Vance’s Iran contact as regional powers push for deal President Donald Trump said Washington is communicating with Iran through mediators, as regional governments seek to revive peace negotiations and avert renewed US strikes. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei at Trump’s direction. Asked about the contact, Trump said he had approved Vance’s request to help Iran obtain medical supplies. “Basically, it’s getting supplies in to help people that are not well,” he said. Qatar-led mediators are urging Tehran to allow UN inspectors into bombed nuclear sites in exchange for some US sanctions relief, Axios reported. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Türkiye are supporting the effort. Trump said he did not know whether negotiations would succeed. Trump also had a phone call with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who told him that the Mecca Joint Defense Alliance was closely monitoring developments in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen. - Spain begins three days of mourning after deadly train crash Spain is in three days of mourning after Wednesday's collision between two high-speed trains killed at least 68 people, one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's recent history. Speaking at the crash site in Toledo, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said authorities would determine the cause of the accident and take action if wrongdoing was uncovered. Sanchez said it was "unacceptable" for a country like Spain to experience two high-speed rail accidents in a single year, referring to January's deadly derailment that claimed the lives of 46 people. "We will get to the bottom of this. If there has been negligence, it will be known," he said, according to Spanish news agency EFE. - Tensions rise as North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles North Korea launched around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, on Thursday, South Korea’s military said. Seoul stepped up surveillance for further launches and shared information with the US and Japan as officials assessed the missiles’ flight distances and other details, Yonhap News reported. Hours earlier, the Japanese Defense Ministry said Pyongyang had fired "what may be a ballistic missile." That prompted a warning from Japan’s Coast Guard urging ships to avoid any fallen objects, Kyodo News reported. - Flavio Bolsonaro lands in US, declares himself Brazil's leader Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami from Ecuador, despite a court order requiring him to surrender his passports as part of a corruption and money-laundering investigation, according to US media reports. He also published a letter on social media describing himself as the country’s "leader" and vowed to lead the opposition to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva from exile in the US. The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro is under investigation over his alleged links to a banker accused of financial misconduct and a man suspected of money laundering.

The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies. The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January. “Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of mourning. Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.

items.title: Analysis-Fed highlights economic strength but muddies outlook for Treasuries By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Oct 29, 2026, 01:05 AM Updated Oct 29, 2026, 01:18 AM By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss and Laura Matthews NEW YORK, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady on Wednesday as expected, but it was not able to comfort bond investors concerned about what a deliberate pace of policy tightening will mean for the outlook for longer-term government bonds. The central bank described an economy strong enough to keep inflation elevated, yet refrained from raising rates immediately. That deepened uncertainty over how much further policy may need to tighten, analysts said, and over how much compensation investors could demand to hold longer-dated Treasuries, which have soared this year to their highest yields in two decades. The Fed upgraded its assessment of the economy to "strong" from the "solid" expansion seen as of the September meeting, while describing investment as robust and job gains as keeping pace with the workforce. But how that all leads to price pressures coming down - the main priority for bond investors - was less clear. "Ultimately, if we see strong growth, which (Fed Chair Kevin) Warsh is expecting, we’re going to see more inflation, which means those fiscal deficit concerns and how to address them longer term become more relevant," said Anders Persson, chief investment officer for global fixed income at investment manager Nuveen in Charlotte, North Carolina. LOOKING AHEAD TO MORE COMPLICATED TIMES A combination of resilient economic growth and persistent inflation could complicate the US fiscal outlook, limiting the Fed’s ability to lower interest rates when the economy turns and keeping Treasury borrowing costs elevated. The yield curve steepened following Warsh’s press conference, with the long end selling off. The spread between 2- and 10-year yields widened to as much as 34.1 basis points after flattening over the last few weeks. There were different interpretations as to why. One was that Warsh did not give a definitive commitment on future policy action, which reduced rate-hike bets. He also suggested the Fed’s last rate increase is starting to work and that financial conditions have started to tighten. The resulting steepening of the US Treasury yield curve, however, underscores the growing tension between a Fed that is willing to wait for more evidence before adjusting policy and investors increasingly concerned about persistent price pressures and the risks of holding long-term government debt. Treasury yields have climbed across most maturities from the belly of the curve - between 5 and 7 years - onwards following the Fed’s latest decision, with longer-dated yields coming under particular pressure. ... Financial markets are already pricing in the possibility of another increase in December, with expectations for further hikes next year adding to uncertainty over the policy outlook. FED MISREADING STRENGTH OF ECONOMY? Market participants also questioned the Fed’s assessment of the economy. "What are they looking at to give the economy an upgrade? The moving average of weekly payroll gains from ADP was trending up between the July and September meeting, but it has been trending down since," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin. "The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow forecast has gone from white hot to merely smoldering," he said. As growth loses some steam, the economy may not need to weaken much to undermine the optimistic outlook, according to some observers. Citigroup’s chief US economist, Andrew Hollenhorst, said Warsh was "overstating the breadth of strength in the US economy, meaning he will likely have a relatively low bar for a downside surprise."

items.title: Fed leaves rates unchanged as it awaits more information
items.excerpt: The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady last night, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said "remains elevated." The 10-2 decisionto maintain the Fed's benchmark interest rate within the 3.75%-4% range came with an upgraded assessment of an economy that the central bank now says is growing at a "strong pace." Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also expressed confidence that inflation can be lowered to the 2% target without having to "throw sand in the gears" and slow growth or raise unemployment. Kevin Warsh, speaking at a press conference after the end of a two-day policy meeting, said he expects a report on third-quarter gross domestic product today to show strong investment and consumer spending and an acceleration of growth from the first half of the year. Warsh, however, said he still does not think the economy is "too hot" or generating demand-side inflation that needs to be curbed. "The economy is pointing in the right direction. Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy running too strong? That isn't the judgment of most of my colleagues," said Warsh, arguing, as he has before, that changes in productivity, even predating the artificial intelligence boom, may allow the US to grow faster without as much inflation. "The goal, in my view isn't to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work. I don't think we have to do that." ... The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee's latest policy statement, however, hinted that more rate hikes may be needed, and some of Warsh's colleagues have been explicit in their concerns that demand, fueled by AI and healthy consumer spending, is starting to drive prices higher. Between now and the next policy meeting in December, "the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2% goal," the FOMC said. "The Committee will deliver price stability."
